# Reading paths {.unnumbered}

This book has four parts, twenty-one chapters, four case studies, and two appendices. Reading it cover-to-cover takes most readers a long weekend. Almost no one needs to. The four paths below cover the four most common reasons people pick this book up; pick the one that matches your current job, read it in order, and skim or skip the rest.

| Path | For | Time | Read in this order |
|------|-----|------|--------------------|
| **Strategic frame** | CEO, CTO, CIO, board member assessing AI-native delivery | ~45 min | Preface → Ch1 (Thesis) → Ch3 (Business case) → Ch6 (Team structures) → Ch7 (Transition) |
| **Engineering leadership** | VP Engineering, Director, Head of Platform building the rollout plan | ~2 hrs | Path 1 → Ch4 (Reference architecture) → Ch5 (Governance) → Ch8 (Part III map) → Ch11 (Instrumented codebase) → Ch16 (Multi-agent orchestration) |
| **Senior practitioner** | Staff/Principal engineer, tech lead designing primitives this week | ~3 hrs | Ch8 (Part III map) → Ch9 (Mindset) → Ch10 (Runtime machine) → Ch11 (Instrumented codebase) → Ch12 (PROSE constraints) → Ch13 (Load lifecycle) → Ch14 (Attention) → Ch20 (Primitives as code) → Appendix A (Cross-harness reference) |
| **Mid-level developer** | 3–5 years experience, shipping with an agent on Monday | ~90 min | Ch9 (Mindset) → Ch12 (PROSE constraints) → Ch13 (Load lifecycle) → Ch14 (Attention) → Ch19 (Anti-patterns) → one Part IV case study that matches your stack |

The four parts are designed to be read in any order; the chapter sequence inside each part is the only place sequence matters. Part IV (case studies) and the appendices stand on their own and can be sampled at any point — the Cross-harness reference (Appendix A) in particular is worth bookmarking before you start, regardless of path.
